title: Rafi and Ember and the Starfall Spark
markdown:
The River Festival was near. This year two friends had the biggest job: lighting the Starfall Lantern. Moon-petal blossoms sweetened the air. Excitement hummed as the sun dipped behind the Emerald Peaks. The lantern was not any festival lamp. It held old magic, a gift meant to bless the year.

Rafi was a raccoon whose whiskers twitched with curiosity and whose paws were quicker than a blink. He loved a challenge. Ember was a paper dragon, scales of delicate parchment that shimmered with a soft warm light. He was thoughtful. He often saw what others missed.

“The Great Elder entrusted us,” Rafi said, thrill and duty mixed. He clutched the lantern: polished moon-stone, gleaming filigree, something like captured starlight pulsing inside. “We must place it by the river before the first star.”

“The current is strong tonight,” Ember whispered. His scales rustled like leaves. “And the wind is a trickster. It might snatch it.” He shivered, not from cold, from wonder.

They set off. Rafi held the lantern in small strong paws. Moonlight dappled the path through ancient trees. A sharp crackle came from the basket. A spark no bigger than a ladybug flickered at the lantern’s base, a trapped firefly trying to leave.

“What was that?” Rafi’s eyes widened. The lantern sighed a puff of warm air across his fur. It felt different.

Fire is a hungry thing. It needs fuel to dance, a spark to start, and air — plenty of it — to grow. The Starfall Lantern, full of ancient heat, was no different. Its light was powerful, and power, even kind power, could be unpredictable.

They hurried into the Whispering Woods. Trees old enough to keep secrets rustled. Another crackle, louder, closer. Rafi stumbled on a gnarled root. The lantern nearly tumbled. He saw then a pile of dry brittle leaves in a forgotten corner of the path, begging for a spark.

“The leaves,” Ember gasped. Paper wings fluttered. “The lantern is too warm for them. Perfect little snacks for a spark.”

Rafi understood. Fuel, waiting. He nudged the leaves away with his snout, heart thrumming. “Careful. Beautiful magic. Powerful heat. Nothing that can catch.”

They came out into the Shimmering Meadow. Tall grasses swayed, an emerald sea dotted with fireflies. Dewy clover and wild mint. Crackle again, more insistent. A thin wisp of smoke curled from the filigree.

“Look.” Ember pointed a paper claw. A tiny orange ember was about to land on parched golden grass. “It needs air to grow. Too much, too close to the fuel…”

Oxygen. They had to reach the river before the spark became a blaze. Rafi bolted, legs a blur. Ember caught a gust — not to fan the lantern, which would feed the rogue coal, but to swoop low as a buffer, nudging dry blades aside, clearing a path.

“Faster! The river is just ahead!”

They reached the bank as the first star pricked the velvet sky. The river was a silver ribbon. The lantern pulsed hard. Sparks like runaway stars flew toward bone-dry reeds. The reeds crackled with potential.

“No!” Rafi dropped to his knees. His treasure-finding paws scrabbled, pushing reeds back from the heat.

Ember hovered, a living shield. Reeds were fuel. Heat was spark. Air was the fan. He angled his wings into a gentle eddy, redirecting sparks — not a fierce blow, a painter’s stroke.

With a last heave Rafi made a gap of damp cool earth between lantern and the worst stalks. Escaped sparks hissed out on moist soil. The frantic crackle subsided. The glow softened into a steady beacon. Promise, not threat.

They set the lantern on a waiting barge. Moon-stone on smooth wood. The barge joined a procession. Other lamps shimmered. Paper streamers danced.

Rafi and Ember stood breathless on the bank, a little weary, quietly glad. Cool sweet air. Distant chatter and soft music. The river mirrored a thousand lights. Ember unfolded his wings, not to fly, to rest. Their edges caught the Starfall glow as the barge began its glide.

“We did it,” Rafi whispered. Whiskers drooped. Eyes shone.

Ember watched the lantern go. He did not name a lesson. He only folded one wing so it would not catch the breeze the wrong way, and the river took the light where the first star had asked it to be.
